common_name: Merion Kentucky Bluegrass (Historic Fine-Textured Golf and Lawn Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow in late summer to early fall into a fertile, well-prepared seedbed; Merion was selected from turf growing at Merion Golf Club in Pennsylvania and became the first widely marketed named Kentucky bluegrass cultivar.

directions: Sow in early fall for the strongest establishment window, since Merion germinates and knits into sod slowly compared with modern turf-type bluegrasses. Selected from a patch of unusually dense, fine-textured turf found growing at Merion Golf Club outside Philadelphia, it was released commercially in the 1950s and set off the modern era of improved Kentucky bluegrass breeding, giving home lawns a denser, lower-growing alternative to common pasture-type seed. It is more prone to leaf spot and melting-out disease under stress than the cultivars that followed it, so maintain consistent fertility and avoid excessive shade or drought. Its chief significance today is historical, as the genetic foundation many later compact-type bluegrasses were bred to improve upon.
sources: Pennsylvania State University Extension — Kentucky Bluegrass History
United States Golf Association Green Section
National Turfgrass Evaluation Program

common_name: Park Kentucky Bluegrass (University of Minnesota Common-Type Lawn Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow in early fall or early spring; Park was released by the University of Minnesota from naturalized bluegrass ecotypes and remains an inexpensive, widely adapted general-purpose lawn seed.

directions: Sow in early fall into a prepared seedbed and keep consistently moist until the stand fills in, which takes longer than with elite modern cultivars. Park was developed by the University of Minnesota from naturalized, winter-hardy bluegrass stands rather than from an elite single selection, giving it broad regional adaptability and exceptional cold tolerance across the northern plains and upper Midwest. Its turf quality, density, and disease resistance are more modest than named compact-type cultivars bred for sports turf or golf, which is reflected in its long history as an economical component of general-purpose lawn and roadside seed mixes. Overseed thin areas in fall and expect it to persist reliably with only routine mowing and fertility.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Lawn Establishment and Renovation
National Turfgrass Evaluation Program

common_name: Glade Kentucky Bluegrass (Shade-Tolerant Dense Compact-Type Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow in early fall into a fertile seedbed; Glade was bred for better shade tolerance than older common-type bluegrass and is often blended with fine fescue for lawns under trees.

directions: Sow in early fall and keep the seedbed evenly moist through the multi-week germination period, favoring sites with filtered or part-day shade where Glade's relative strength over standard bluegrass becomes most apparent. It forms a dense, dark green, compact-type sod and was bred specifically to extend Kentucky bluegrass into lightly shaded lawn areas that would otherwise favor weaker turf, though it still performs best with at least a few hours of direct sun. It has shown good resistance to leaf spot in university trials relative to older cultivars, making it a reasonably low-maintenance choice once established. Blend with shade-tolerant fine fescues for the most reliable results under partial tree canopy.
sources: Rutgers University Center for Turfgrass Science
National Turfgrass Evaluation Program
Pennsylvania State University Extension — Shade-Tolerant Lawn Grasses

common_name: Nugget Kentucky Bluegrass (Early Low-Growing Compact-Type Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow in early fall; Nugget was one of the first low-growing, compact-type Kentucky bluegrass cultivars bred at Oregon State University and requires less frequent mowing than common seed.

directions: Sow in early fall into a firm, fertile seedbed and expect slower initial establishment than common bluegrass. Developed at Oregon State University, Nugget was among the earliest named compact-type bluegrasses, with a notably low, dense growth habit and dark color that reduced mowing frequency compared with older pasture-type seed available at the time. It is more prone to injury from summer heat and certain diseases in warmer transition-zone climates than cultivars bred later, so it performs best in genuinely cool-summer regions. It remains notable as an early parent in the lineage of modern dwarf-type Kentucky bluegrass breeding.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Turfgrass Seed Production
National Turfgrass Evaluation Program

common_name: Fylking Kentucky Bluegrass (Classic Scandinavian-Bred Low-Growing Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow in early fall; Fylking was bred in Sweden and was one of the first dwarf-type Kentucky bluegrasses marketed in North America, valued for its low growth and dark color.

directions: Sow in early fall and irrigate lightly and frequently until the seedlings establish a root system. Bred in Sweden and introduced to North America in the 1960s, Fylking helped popularize the compact, low-growing bluegrass type, offering a finer texture and darker green color than older common seed along with reduced mowing needs. It is noticeably more susceptible to leaf spot and melting-out disease during hot, humid summers than cultivars developed after it, so it performs most reliably in cooler northern climates with good air circulation. Despite being largely superseded by newer releases, it remains historically important as one of the cultivars that launched the modern improved-bluegrass seed market.
sources: National Turfgrass Evaluation Program
University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension — Kentucky Bluegrass Cultivars

common_name: Touchdown Kentucky Bluegrass (Dark Green Aggressive Compact-Type Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow in early fall into a fertile seedbed; Touchdown became an influential compact-type Kentucky bluegrass known for dark color and aggressive rhizome spread, and has been used as a parent in later breeding.

directions: Sow in early fall and keep the bed evenly moist through the slow multi-week germination process typical of the species. Touchdown is a compact-type Kentucky bluegrass noted for dark green color, dense sod formation, and vigorous rhizome spread that helps it self-repair after wear, qualities that made it an influential cultivar in lawn and sports turf seed blends. It performs best with regular mowing and moderate nitrogen fertility to sustain its density without becoming overly thatch-prone. Because of its strong genetics it has also served as a breeding parent for a related family of later compact bluegrass releases.
sources: National Turfgrass Evaluation Program
Oregon State University Extension — Turfgrass Seed Production

common_name: Victa Kentucky Bluegrass (Dark Green Compact-Type Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow in early fall; Victa is a compact-type Kentucky bluegrass closely related to Touchdown, sharing its dark color, dense habit, and self-repairing rhizome spread.

directions: Sow in early fall into a prepared seedbed and water lightly and frequently until germination finishes. Victa shares much of its breeding background with Touchdown, producing a similarly dark green, low, compact-type sod with vigorous rhizome activity that fills in bare spots and wear patterns over time. It was commonly blended with other compact-type and common bluegrasses in lawn and sports turf seed mixes to broaden genetic diversity and disease resistance within a stand. Maintain moderate nitrogen fertility and regular mowing to keep its dense growth from building excess thatch.
sources: National Turfgrass Evaluation Program
Oregon State University Extension — Turfgrass Seed Production

common_name: Bristol Kentucky Bluegrass (Compact Dense Dark-Green Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow in early fall into a fertile, well-drained seedbed; Bristol is a compact-type Kentucky bluegrass bred for dense, dark green turf in home lawn and sports field seed blends.

directions: Sow in early fall and keep the seedbed consistently moist through the slow germination period typical of Kentucky bluegrass. Bristol is one of the compact-type cultivars developed alongside Baron and America during the push to improve on older common bluegrass seed, producing a dense, dark green, relatively low-growing sod well suited to home lawns and general-purpose sports turf. It is commonly blended with other elite bluegrass cultivars to combine disease resistance genes from different sources within the same stand. Mow regularly at a moderate height and provide consistent nitrogen fertility to maintain its density through the growing season.
sources: National Turfgrass Evaluation Program
Pennsylvania State University Extension — Kentucky Bluegrass Cultivars

common_name: Santa Ana Bermudagrass (Classic Fine-Textured California Hybrid Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Install as sod, sprigs, or plugs from spring through midsummer; Santa Ana is a sterile hybrid bermudagrass propagated only vegetatively, developed in California for fine-textured golf and park turf.

directions: Plant sprigs or lay sod in a full-sun site and irrigate consistently during the two- to three-week knitting period before tapering to deep, infrequent watering. Santa Ana was developed in California in the 1950s as one of the early fine-textured hybrid bermudagrasses for golf courses, parks, and sports fields, prized for its dense, dark green sod and better cold tolerance than many finer ornamental bermuda selections of the time. It wears well under traffic and recovers quickly from scalping or divots, though it still goes fully dormant and straw-colored after the first hard freeze. As with other hybrid bermudas, it needs regular mowing, fertility, and full sun to hold its fine texture and density.
sources: University of California Division of Agriculture and Natural Resources
National Turfgrass Evaluation Program

common_name: U-3 Bermudagrass (Classic Cold-Hardy Vegetative Turf Selection)

planting.note: Install as sod, sprigs, or plugs from spring through midsummer; U-3 is an older vegetatively propagated common-type bermudagrass long valued for cold tolerance in the transition zone.

directions: Plant sprigs or plugs into a full-sun site in late spring and keep the planting consistently moist until runners knit into a solid stand. U-3 is one of the older named common-type bermudagrass selections, long used across the transition zone for its ability to survive winters that kill out less cold-hardy bermudagrass, making it a historically important cultivar before the development of modern cold-tolerant hybrids like Patriot and NorthBridge. Its texture and density are coarser than improved hybrids, and it spreads aggressively by both rhizomes and stolons, so plan mowing edges and borders accordingly. It still turns brown with the first hard frost and greens back up reliably once soil warms in spring.
sources: Oklahoma State University Extension — Bermudagrass Variety History
National Turfgrass Evaluation Program

common_name: UF-Riata Bahiagrass (University of Florida Low-Growing Fine-Textured Lawn Cultivar)

planting.note: Direct sow scarified seed once soil is consistently warm; UF-Riata was bred at the University of Florida for a lower, finer growth habit and fewer seedheads than Argentine or Pensacola bahiagrass.

directions: Sow scarified seed after the last frost once soil has warmed, watering lightly and frequently until the stand germinates and fills in. UF-Riata was bred at the University of Florida to combine the deep-rooted drought tolerance of standard bahiagrass with a lower, more compact growth habit and reduced seedhead production, giving it a tidier, more lawn-like appearance that needs less frequent mowing than Argentine or Pensacola types. It tolerates the same poor, sandy, infertile soils that make bahiagrass popular across the Gulf South, requiring minimal fertilizer once established. Mow regularly through the growing season even though seedhead production is reduced, and expect it to go dormant and brown after the first hard frost.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bahiagrass Lawn Management
National Turfgrass Evaluation Program

common_name: Competidora Bahiagrass (Texas-Bred Improved Forage and Pasture Cultivar)

planting.note: Direct sow scarified seed once soil is consistently warm; Competidora is a Texas-bred bahiagrass selected for improved forage yield and later seasonal maturity than Pensacola.

directions: Sow scarified seed after the last frost once soil has warmed, keeping the seedbed moist through the slow two- to four-week germination period. Competidora was developed by Texas A&M AgriLife to extend the bahiagrass growing season with later fall maturity and improved forage yield compared with Pensacola, making it more of a pasture and hay grass than a fine lawn turf, though it shares the same deep, drought-tolerant root system. It performs reliably on poor, sandy, acidic soils across the southern Gulf states with minimal fertility input. Mow or graze regularly through the growing season to manage its tall seed stalks and keep stands productive.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Bahiagrass Forage Variety Trials
National Turfgrass Evaluation Program
